en: The Ritual Manual for the Yoga Contemplation of the Sovereign One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa Cakra King, in one fascicle.
By the Grand Master of the Household, Peer of the State, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery, who was the Duke of Sù with a fief of three thousand households, recipient of the purple robe, posthumously honored as Minister of Works, and bestowed the title Dàjiàn (Great Mirror) and the epithet Dàguǎngzhì (Great Universal Wisdom). If a practitioner of the mantra-path seeks *āntardhāna* (invisibility), [they should proceed as follows].
One should form this thought:
"How may I swiftly attain accomplishment?
I shall practice this samādhi."
One should form such a resolute conviction: that all phenomena are formless,
being spontaneously accomplished by their very nature as the nature of space.
One should purify the ground and so forth according to the original teachings and perform this samādhi:
pervading the trichiliocosm, it fills all with the water of wisdom.
There is a great precious lotus flower, blooming within the water;
its precious stem is like Mount Sumeru. Above it, a net of jewels covers the flower, and upon it are great treasures adorned with eight pillars.
Visualize a jeweled pavilion with four gates facing the four directions,
adorned with nets of pearls, lotuses, and bells, as well as exquisite whisks;
it is further embellished with crescent and full moon shapes, pearl necklaces, and hanging bands of various jewels interspersed throughout.
This great jewel pavilion fills all the way to the Peak of Existence;
one should contemplate it according to one's capacity.
Within the previously visualized pavilion, one should observe an ocean-like cloud of offerings, featuring a pleasing white parasol.
Adorned with various precious ornaments, such as jeweled necklaces, half-moon shapes,
and exquisite whisks, the parasol above is graced by a great jewel that radiates light everywhere,
raining down a profusion of various treasures.
Through the practice of mantra-wisdom contemplation,
one dwells upon that pavilion atop a vajra-lion throne, adorned with precious lotuses,
jeweled nets, lotus-silk streamers, and bells, as well as white whisks and other ornaments.
All those who delight in desire and pleasure surround [the central figure], dwelling not far from his body. One should visualize a second seat;
everything is as described above, with the sole exception that there is no lion throne.
At the four corners of the gate, one performs the rites of play, burning incense, and so forth;
next, the ritual for full ordination (*upasampadā*) is performed. How is the full ordination performed?
First, one should contemplate all phenomena: that their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is their very self-nature.
When self and others are realized as one and the same essence, one can then apply this to all phenomena.
How is it applied to all phenomena? Birth, aging, sickness, sorrow, and death agitate the field of the mind; having reflected in this way, [one applies it].
One should give rise to great compassion; from this, the mind of wisdom is born.
Perfumed by great compassion, its essence is like the full moon, free from subject and object; thus, the bodhicitta has been generated.
One should abide in body, speech, and mind; the empowerment of the essence that is thus clarified constitutes the King of the Family.
First, one should form the seal, which is called the Great Seal (mahāmudrā).
Next, the visualization to be contemplated is explained: by means of the essence of body, speech, and mind.
One should imagine one's own body as all Buddhas; within the mind, one should visualize a stainless lunar disc like a Buddha.
The mantra practitioner should know that there are various kinds of light rays, all of which arise from the form of the moon.
Pervading the infinite realms, it enters again; the practitioner’s mind is firm and steadfast.
It forms five peaks and transforms into the shape of a vajra, which one visualizes within one's own palm, from which various rays of light then emanate.
That light pervades everywhere, reaching as far as the boundless realms,
where it performs the Buddha’s playful manifestations; returning once more to the body of Yukhi,
it enters therein in this manner and becomes the great color of Samantabhadra.
One should contemplate the Great Bodhisattva, whose various marks are all perfected and who possesses every ornament; the Mahāsattva, crowned with a lotus garland,
is spontaneously accomplished from the mind of yoga.
Holding the bow and arrow of mantras, abiding upon a moon disc or holding a garland;
or else, dwelling in the four directions, one should visualize before oneself,
according to one's capacity, the great bliss of all sentient beings.
The Supreme Accomplishment: All mudrās adorn her hands as she bestows gifts upon all sentient beings;
according to their wishes, she dances with joy, and from her, the Vajramālā flows forth.
With the left hand at the side of the waist and the right hand held in a dancing gesture,
he establishes the benefit of all sentient beings. Just as his own radiance appears according to the forms of those who behold him, he causes them all to attain subdual.
Performing such empowerment, one brings benefit to sentient beings and other various benefits;
having merely presented offerings such as *lāja* and so forth,
one honors oneself as the venerable one.
The syllables of the mantra correspond [to one another]; recite them according to one's capacity.
Just as sound corresponds to form, the wise should contemplate the syllables as a flower garland, in accordance with the yoga of correspondence.
Regarding sound, I shall now explain: all that is most excellent is established as the Tathāgata Lotus Family.
Reciting with the sound of a conch shell, I praise it like the roar of thunder; clearly pronounce the syllable HŪṂ.
I say that the Vajra family also extends to Maheśvara.
For the practitioner of recitation, there is the accomplishment of the southern maṇi-karma;
this is the recitation of this family.
Like the sound of a bell or a chime;
like the sound of a lute, a flute,
or the tinkling of dancing ornaments.
Its sound is like the cry of a peacock;
it accords with all meanings within the teachings of all sections.
Producing such sounds,
one performs the recitation in accordance with the mantra.
The mantra practitioner should contemplate its meaning in accordance with the sound;
before long, they shall attain accomplishment.
This applies to all sections; this is the ritual procedure for the recitation of sound.
I shall speak of the recitation of form;
I now speak of everything.
Form is said to be the seal;
its corresponding transformation is called movement. One should contemplate its luminosity well and place it upon the breast.
Observing with the seal of radiant light,
vajras emerge from within the body,
which are then sprinkled with nectar.
Causing the original deities to rejoice and enabling one to conceal one's own form— this,
O Great Hero, I have taught.
Those who perform the recitation of forms by means of this mantra shall know that they will achieve accomplishment through the mudrās;
before long, they will easily change their bodies.
I shall explain yoga.
One should perform the recitation as previously described,
and one should contemplate the vidyā-mantra.
Establish [the deity] in its own place and make offerings according to the instructions.
Perform the recitation with pure and corresponding mindfulness, free from the mind, throat, crown, tongue, nose, and uvula, and free from internal or external conceptualization.
It is merely the correspondence of phenomena;
one should not rely on sounds.
This is called the Vajra.
The Ritual for Yoga Recitation:
If one knows the true essence,
one should know that accomplishment will follow.
And having attained permanence,
one dwells in accordance with this yoga method.
By means of the supreme mind of bodhicitta,
before long they shall all achieve success and obtain their every wish.
Regarding the recitation of the syllables therein,
I shall now explain it as I have attained it;
thus one accumulates the provisions.
One should recite and maintain the mantra;
one should contemplate it by distinguishing its colors according to the syllables.
Performing the rite of recitation,
one generates the moon-disk with a focused mind;
the syllable of light arises together with it.
Place the principal deity upon one's chest;
before long, one will attain the *āttadāna*.
Regarding the moon, join it with the moon.
Regarding all syllables and forms,
one should contemplate above them the adornment of the wheel of light.
The rows are uninterrupted,
like pearls strung on a thread,
with golden light as their radiance.
The body of the Honored One shines brilliantly,
like those various moon-syllables;
such is the supreme and wondrous mantra.
For one who has accomplished the mantra,
there will be joy in each respective case;
their power and life-force will increase and become even more flourishing.
I say that the correspondence with the radiance of the mind is the recitation of the arrangement of syllables.
I now proclaim for the practitioner who recites the vidyā and performs the recitation:
the radiance that accomplishes all ritual procedures.
If one performs that [rite] by means of accomplishing all objects with light,
one should generate the ritual corresponding to recitation;
then all mantras will be accomplished.
The single rite is in accord with the yoga;
one should effect the purification of consciousness.
Purification constitutes the mind-consciousness.
The wise person should indeed enter into accomplishment;
by means of body, speech, and mind,
they abide relying upon such things as these.
One should know the four-limbed dharma;
through the accomplishment of the yoga-dharma,
this is here called "mind."
Having attained the supernormal powers, the stages,
and so forth, he manifests various bodies with his own body according to the inclinations and desires of sentient beings;
with his speech, he elucidates all things.
The accomplishment of smoke, flames, and so forth—
I call this the accomplishment of objects.
Within that, the accomplishment of the body is as follows:
There are many varieties:
the four seals (*mudrā*) and other maṇḍala wheels.
The yogin should construct the great maṇḍala according to his full understanding.
Having accomplished the maṇḍala ritual, one should assume the central samādhi-form.
One should sit upon a soft cushion in the western direction, or else upon a red sika deer skin with a woolen cloth and flowers placed upon it.
And he sits calmly.
All yogas are associated with *samādhi*; "equipoise" (*samāpatti*) refers to entering meditative absorption. The mantra practitioner abides in association with wisdom and mindfulness.
At midnight, or when the dawn light appears, or at the third watch,
or when the dawn light is certain to appear, one shall achieve accomplishment;
or one achieves mastery over the earth and the supernormal powers.
The Tathāgata has spoken;
I now declare that the accomplishment of the mind is attained by manifesting the body.
Empower the body with this seal.
One should reflect thus: "I am now the Great Seal."
Regarding those who practice the recitation of mantras within the maṇḍala for the sake of accomplishment,
accomplishment is attained through a pure mind;
I shall now describe the signs of accomplishment.
If light, warmth, smoke, or an increase [of size] issues from the mouth or body,
or if one sees oneself ascending into the sky,
one should know that these are signs of accomplishment corresponding to the bodily accomplishment (*kāyasiddhi*).
I have finished my extensive exposition.
I shall now explain the method for accomplishing speech,
as it is taught according to its successive stages.
Having performed the preliminary rites, one should proceed according to the previous method:
having established oneself, one should abide upon a lotus flower atop the seals of body, speech, and mind, up to and including the Great Seal (mahāmudrā).
One should know that within the heart, above [it], there resides a conch (śaṅkha), which means it is upon the flower; from within the conch, sound issues forth in an uninterrupted continuity.
Within the lotus, a vajra-tongue is produced.
Regarding that which is white, one visualizes it as red; upon it, one visualizes a vajra-tongue, or a Buddha, or a jewel, or a lotus, or a karma-vajra, or the mudrā of another family.
One should perform the visualization for one month, two months, three, four, or five months, up to eight months.
Seated in the full lotus posture upon this maṇḍala,
one should always remain in union with the primordial quiescence.
Having clearly observed the sound of the conch shell,
one then relies upon the lotus realm;
from the filaments of the flower, there emerges a sound as subtle as a mote of dust.
The sound emerges at the throat,
then reaches the tongue,
and immediately forms the character.
From the syllable *jihvā* (tongue) there issues a blaze of light;
the flames are fierce and all-pervading,
filling the void with sound.
The practitioner, with focused concentration, recites for one day and one night;
during the middle watch or the latter watch of the night,
light radiates from the tongue.
That light produced a great sound;
from the heart, the lips, and the teeth,
it emitted an intermingled radiance.
If one sees such [signs], one should know that siddhi has been attained.
By corresponding with these words, one can refute the various heterodox schools, cause others to develop pure faith,
and bring benefit to sentient beings.
Thus, through recitation in accordance with yoga,
the bhikṣu Vāgacchatra shall attain the accomplishment of speech.
Emerging amidst these interspersed [teachings],
the ritual procedures for the accomplishment of speech are perfected over seven days.
I shall now explain the accomplishment of material substances.
One should accomplish it according to the yoga described previously.

One should take materials from another *tantra* or use a mudrā and mantra from another *tantra*—that is, with a ladle (*śarāva*), one should pour all the substances into the fire-pit; and when the remaining sounds have not yet ceased, one should again perform the ritual procedure for the substances.
The wise one enters the *karmasamaya* of this maṇḍala and personally performs all ritual actions (*karma*).
Exercising mastery therein constitutes the physical form (rūpalakṣaṇa).
For all [deities] within their respective families,
one should sequentially bestow the hand-seals (mudrā) and ritual objects (vastu) upon the lords of those families.
Place the object within the vajra-bond;
pile up the various types [of objects] therein.
The binding mudrā should be positioned below the navel or at the heart.
Binding the two hands together, one offers them as a tribute to the peaceful state within one's own mind;
this is the self-illumination.
By means of this method, the wise one [attains realization].
Visualize the body as a mass of fire.
Taking the previously accumulated provisions of merit from body, speech, and mind, use these bodily substances and place them in the hand of the Wisdom-Being (vidyā).
The practitioner of mantras should perform the recitation of the mantra syllables, their flames, and their sounds throughout the entire night;
they must not break their meditative posture.
By means of this ritual procedure,
warmth shall arise during the first watch of the night,
and smoke shall appear during the middle watch.
Just as a flame increases its radiance through the stages of light and appearance,
so too does it gradually augment itself until,
like a flame, it brings the object into being.
One attains the power to soar through the void and gains mastery over the three realms;
this I call the *āśvāsana* (soothing) rite.
I have already stated before:
one should sever all grasping and rely upon the fundamental luminosity.
This extends even to one's own body;
the same applies to speech and mind.
By means of one's own mantra.
One should cause [the deity] to vanish and act as the presiding lord of the root vidyā;
one should perform the recitation.
This is the name of the Great Vajra.
With the great vajra body,
the wise one should firmly abide in summoning, binding, and pleasing [the deity],
and should place it within the heart.
Just as one’s own mind desires,
I clearly contemplate my own body:
"I am empty space."
Through this accomplishment of union,
even up to the lords of the entire desire realm,
they do not perceive his form.
In an instant, one reaches the Brahma-heaven;
having exhausted that dharma, one performs the summoning.
One should construct a maṇḍala of four seals.
One should place the mind upon the left hand;
placing oneself within it,
one should firmly grasp it with the fist.
Forming a fist as the void,
one establishes the *antaḥpura* in this manner;
even the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa gods cannot perceive it.
He roams through the Palace of Mastery over Others' Emanations,
enjoying at will all forms of peace, bliss, and sovereignty, even those desired by the mind.
This is the method for placing the medicinal pill in the mouth and the *taṭāna* rite.
I shall now briefly explain the method for accomplishment.
Thus one contemplates one’s own vidyā:
"I am the essence of all, which means being of one body with that which is to be accomplished within space. One's own body becomes identical to that mudrā.
Abiding in the subtle vajra-samādhi,
one enters the self-luminous mind;
thus, the pill medicine is accomplished.
Visualize a medicinal pill placed in the mouth;
one can travel to the summit of Mount Sumeru,
unseen by anyone in all the worlds.

The color of the medicine produces great power, meaning that the body transforms at will; one experiences the sensual pleasures of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and attains happiness according to one's desire.
This is distinct from other worldly conditions of intermingling.
I shall now explain the *āntardāna*.
Pills are prepared according to the original teachings;
through the wisdom of mantras, one should perform the self-clarification (*svavidyā*).
One who seeks the body of wisdom should offer this to the Accomplished One,
which is stainless like space.
One clearly visualizes the body, objects, and forms,
arranged in rows of syllables,
abiding in conjunction with blazing flames.
One should enter the body of the deity,
dwelling there with a mind as if vanished; then,
from the mouth of the luminosity, it flows forth.
The light of the mantra is majestic and fierce;
the medicinal pills will successfully be accomplished once the smoke has arisen and billowed upward.
Having prohibited [the speech] and brought peace to the mouth,
one attains mastery within the unmanifest form and wanders through the four continents.
In a single kṣaṇa, all worlds return to their original places;
wherever they go, they do so according to their will.
Accomplishing various feats,
he is constantly accompanied by hosts of yakṣas as his retinue;
he is also able to sport within the four yakṣa worlds beneath the four tiers of Mount Sumeru, bringing benefit to immeasurable sentient beings.
Lost on the right path and adrift in the wilderness, they are beset by bandits, kings, water, fire, and the like.
Toward all those in such states of bondage, I give rise to this heart of compassion:
"I shall bring them to fulfillment so that they may all attain liberation."
I have now briefly explained this;
the extensive teaching is as found in the great sūtras.
One should contemplate the moon within one's own mind.
The moon’s form is endowed with radiance; within this moon,
there is a single syllable like the color of gold.
Difficult to behold, like the orb of the sun,
its radiance extends everywhere;
the practitioner of yoga should contemplate this radiance.
Thus its character is that of a wheel;
this wheel is a "turning wheel" (cakravartin),
possessing a wondrous form and color, and surrounded by the seven treasures.
From every pore of his body,
immeasurable Buddhas flow forth;
the practitioner of yoga should contemplate this.
Using the Vajradhātu mudrā,
empower the four places by reciting the mantra; through this,
the power of diligence is accomplished.
With mindfulness and concentration as fuel for diligence,
burn away all transgressions by means of the fire of mantra-colors.
One should abandon doubt and discrimination;
seek great bliss and renounce minor pleasures;
and with earnest wisdom, pursue awakening.
The Ritual Manual for the Yoga and Contemplative Practice of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King, Residing in the Rules of Mantra. One fascicle.
